cim: Sterile Supply Nurses Show Diverse Preferences for Artificial Intelligence Training Formats
cim_eredeti: Sterile Supply Nurses Show Diverse Preferences for Artificial Intelligence Training Formats
szoveg_eredeti:
Sterile Supply Nurses Show Diverse Preferences for Artificial Intelligence Training Formats

A cross-sectional investigation evaluating artificial intelligence training preferences among central sterile supply department nurses found that staff members favored multiple instructional formats rather than a single teaching method. In the survey of 1,141 nurses, traditional offline lectures and online pre-recorded courses emerged as the most widely selected options, while blended training, hands-on workshops, and live-streamed sessions also attracted substantial support across the surveyed workforce.

The research was conducted as a secondary analysis of survey data gathered in August 2026 to assess artificial intelligence teaching cognition among central sterile supply department personnel. The administered questionnaire evaluated general participant information, self-reported artificial intelligence cognition and attitudes, current applications of artificial intelligence in teaching environments, overall demand for artificial intelligence instruction, and specific format preferences. The investigators analyzed valid responses using descriptive statistics, Student t tests, chi-square tests, and multivariate logistic regression models, addressing missing data through an available-case analysis framework.

Preferences for instructional modalities were distributed across five primary formats, with each respondent choosing an average of 3.40 ± 1.28 formats. Centralized offline lectures ranked highest, selected by 820 participants or 71.87 percent of respondents. Online pre-recorded courses followed closely, preferred by 811 nurses, representing 71.08 percent. Blended training was endorsed by 772 nurses, or 67.66 percent, while practical workshops or training camps were favored by 753 nurses, or 65.99 percent. Online live-streamed courses were preferred by 722 nurses, accounting for 63.28 percent of the cohort.

The survey also quantified participant assessments across several related instructional dimensions using numerical scoring scales. Across the study cohort of 1,141 nurses, the mean score for self-reported artificial intelligence cognition and attitudes was 38.34 ± 7.72. The average score measuring the current application of artificial intelligence in teaching reached 27.82 ± 7.53, while the mean score reflecting specific demand for artificial intelligence teaching and training was recorded at 35.67 ± 7.92.

The investigators evaluated differences between nurses who favored blended training modalities and those who did not. Comparative univariate testing revealed that nurses selecting blended instruction differed to a statistically significant degree from non-selecting colleagues in their self-reported artificial intelligence cognition and attitude scores, their instructional demand scores, and their sex distribution, with each comparison reaching statistical significance at a probability value below 0.05.

Multivariate logistic regression modeling confirmed that these variables remained independently associated with a preference for blended instructional programs. Higher self-reported artificial intelligence cognition and attitude scores were positively associated with selecting blended training, yielding an odds ratio of 1.070 with a 95 percent confidence interval spanning 1.051 to 1.089. Elevated demand scores similarly correlated with blended training preferences, showing an odds ratio of 1.081 with a 95 percent confidence interval from 1.062 to 1.100. Sex was also significantly associated with the preference, exhibiting an odds ratio of 0.438 with a 95 percent confidence interval between 0.200 and 0.958. Calibration testing using the Hosmer-Lemeshow method demonstrated good model fit with a probability value exceeding 0.05, and the receiver operating characteristic curve analysis demonstrated an area under the curve of 0.685.

In their assessment of the findings, the study authors concluded that central sterile supply department nurses maintain diverse preferences for artificial intelligence educational formats rather than uniform instructional needs. The authors highlighted that future educational programs should consider underlying population heterogeneity, specifically accounting for variations in age structure, digital literacy, and occupational job roles. They suggested that blended training represents one viable instructional pathway alongside other favored options, while noting that broader implementation should follow rigorous feasibility assessments and prospective evaluations of educational outcomes.

Subject of Research: Artificial intelligence teaching format preferences among central sterile supply department nurses

Article Title: Preferences for artificial intelligence teaching and training formats among nurses in central sterile supply departments and associated factors

Article References: Zhou, J., Li, A., Hu, L., Li, J., Huang, X., Wang, Y., Huang, X., & Cheng, S. (2026). Preferences for artificial intelligence teaching and training formats among nurses in central sterile supply departments and associated factors. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-10881-9
